assessment: Five wishes, and the sim priced them for you: by turn 10 you assemble one of your two kills in 4.6% of games on your own draws, and in 31.4% once a tutor is allowed to fetch the missing half. That 27-point gap IS these five slots. Nothing else in the 99 buys a number like it, and it is why this section is the deck's instruction manual and not a footnote. Now spend them correctly. The deck finds its own staples without help: renewable fodder is in hand by turn 10 in 78.6% of games unassisted, a free sacrifice outlet in 78.0%, an ignition source in 73.5%, and Yawgmoth himself casts by turn 6 in 91.3% at a mean of turn 4.29. Those classes do not need a wish. Two things do: Nest of Scarabs, the singleton hub every loop routes through, and a drain — the drain class is 60.8% unassisted, the lowest number on the sheet that the engine actually needs. Fetch the RIGHT drain. Carry this one to every table. On the same verified board, Bastion of Remembrance removes 7 life from each opponent, 28 across the pod (stack 002); Zulaport Cutthroat does the same 7 / 28 (stack 003); Blood Artist removes EIGHT LIFE TOTAL (stack 004, checker verdict: not a kill, and not even close). That is a 3.5x penalty for 'target player' over 'each opponent'. Fetching Blood Artist as your payoff is the single most expensive mistake this section can save you from. Then know your delivery speeds, because they decide when each wish is live. Demonic Tutor and Diabolic Intent put the card in your HAND. Vampiric Tutor and Insatiable Avarice put it on TOP — appointments, not arrivals. Vampiric is an instant, so fire it at the end step before your turn and the transit costs you nothing; Avarice is a sorcery whose tutor mode is +{2} on top of {B}, a three-mana wish that lands next draw. Beseech the Mirror is four mana and, bargained, CASTS the card free at mana value 4 or less — which is every piece that matters except Mikaeus. One cap to keep you honest: a tutor is only as good as its arrival, and you draw one of the five in 61.7% of games by turn 10, mean turn 3.10. Every assisted figure above already lives inside that ceiling. And one standing order before any kill fetch: count bodies first. Stack 001 proved the Blowfly loop unbounded and then named its price — the drain plus TWO other creatures on the battlefield when it starts. Short a body, the wish is a three-mana enchantment that does nothing. Count, then wish, then win.

targets.scenario: End step of the opponent before you, turn 3 or 4. Yawgmoth is down or coming down next turn — 72.1% of goldfish games cast him exactly on turn four. You have fodder and a sacrifice outlet. What you do not have is the hub.
targets.why: The cheapest route to the card the whole deck is built around. One black mana at instant speed on someone else's turn means your own turn stays completely free to cast the three-drop you just booked. Nest is what makes the loop body-neutral instead of body-negative: stack 004 spells the arithmetic out — without a counter landing on something that lives, two of your creatures leave and Nest returns one. Fetch it before anything else and every later wish gets cheaper.

targets.scenario: Yawgmoth and Nest of Scarabs are both on the battlefield, four or five bodies around them, and the table is at healthy life totals. Nothing converts deaths into damage yet.
targets.why: The drain is the class the deck genuinely fails at — 60.8% unassisted against 78.6% for fodder — so this is a wish worth spending. Fetch Bastion specifically. It removes 7 life from EACH opponent on the verified board (stack 002), 28 across the pod, and 8 / 32 if you spend {B}{B} and a discard on Yawgmoth's proliferate. It is an enchantment, so the creature removal pointed at your board cannot touch it, and it arrives with a 1/1 Human Soldier token — one more body is one more activation. Blood Artist is the same slot for 8 total life (stack 004). Do not take the 3.5x pay cut.

citations.quote: wide alpha strikes, loops, commander-damage kills, and each-opponent drains are the payoffs that actually scale

targets.scenario: Player 3 is the combo deck. They untap into six mana with two cards in hand and have been quietly assembling all game. You have {B} open and a stocked board.
targets.why: Your worst matchup is combo, and the interaction suite is four answers that all target a creature. Vampiric at their end step books Rollick onto your draw; you cast it for ZERO with your commander on the battlefield and still deploy your whole turn. This is the wish you make early rather than perfectly — the answer you save is the answer you never cast.

citations.quote: held answers rot — against combo, or lethal already on board, the last profitable moment is now

targets.scenario: Turn 5, three lands, you missed your drop last turn — the sim hits the turn-5 land drop only 68.9% of the time. Your hand holds a four-drop you cannot cast and a spare body on board.
targets.why: The wish nobody at the table expects, because nobody tutors a land with Vampiric. Vampiric searches for a card, not a spell, so the Tower is fair game: it fixes the drop AND it is a free sacrifice outlet that turns any body into {B}{B}. That is engine mana and a land in one slot, on a turn where the alternative was holding a card you cannot cast. Take the land. The kill still needs a turn to be alive for.

tutors.notes: Two life is not free in this deck. You are already paying Yawgmoth 1 per activation, plus Bitterblossom, Necropotence, Black Market Connections, City of Brass, Ancient Tomb, Cabal Pit and Ifnir Deadlands. Cast Vampiric while your total is comfortable, and remember it is an instant — the end step before your turn is almost always the right moment.

targets.scenario: Turn 5 or 6, your own main phase. Yawgmoth is on the battlefield, bodies are flowing, and you have six mana. Nest of Scarabs is nowhere.
targets.why: Your strongest unconditional wish, spent on the deck's most irreplaceable card. Three mana finds it and three mana casts it in the same turn once you are at six — mean available mana is 5.24 on turn six and 6.24 on turn eight, so this is a real sequence, not a fantasy. Nest is the hub both kills share, and the tutor is exactly what makes a singleton behave like a playset.

citations.quote: k tutors plus the card act like k+1 copies of *every* card

targets.scenario: Yawgmoth has been killed twice. He is in your graveyard rather than the command zone, the tax is climbing, and Player 2 still holds up removal every turn.
targets.why: The behind fetch, and it is a rebuild rather than a haymaker. One black mana buys an enchantment that returns Yawgmoth — or any creature — from graveyard to hand for {1}{B} and 2 life, forever, at instant speed. That is the commander tax deleted and every removal spell they own turned into a two-mana inconvenience. Against a table that has decided you are the threat, the card that answers the SECOND and third removal spell is worth more than the card that wins if nobody interacts.

targets.scenario: Nest of Scarabs is on the battlefield. An each-opponent drain is on the battlefield. You have three spare creatures beyond the drain and enough mana to cast a three-drop. Nobody is holding up enchantment removal.
targets.why: This is the closing fetch, and the board state above is not decoration — it is the price stack 001 named. The Blowfly plus Nest loop is genuinely unbounded, but on a board where the drain was the only spare creature it drained for THREE and stalled, because Blowfly's trigger is mandatory and had to eat the payoff. With the drainer plus two other creatures, 38 completed iterations take four opponents from 40 to 0. Count the bodies out loud before you tap. Coaching call: Bastion of Remembrance is the safest partner here precisely because it is an enchantment and Blowfly can never be forced to target it — that reading is judgement built on stack 001's finding, not a separately verified line.

targets.scenario: Turn 7. You have six bodies on the battlefield — the sim's mean is 4.80 by turn seven — an empty hand, and no engine online yet. The board is ahead of the hand.
targets.why: The wish that turns a board into a hand. Every token you make is a 1/1: equip for one, it becomes a 2/0, dies immediately, and you draw two. That is a one-mana artifact refilling you at two cards a body while your drains meter every death. One precision point to keep you out of trouble at the table: Skullclamp's +1/-1 is a static modification, not a counter, so it does NOT trigger Nest of Scarabs. Clamp for cards, not for Insects.

tutors.notes: No conditions, no delay, no life. This is the tutor you fire at the first genuine hole rather than saving for a cleverer turn — and per the strategy on tutoring, the cost you are paying is board impact and a turn of tempo, which means the card you name has to be worth a turn.

targets.scenario: Turn 4 or 5. Bitterblossom has been making a Faerie every upkeep, or Nest has left you an Insect, or Ophiomancer's Snake is sitting there doing nothing. Yawgmoth is down and the table is at 40.
targets.why: The default Intent, because the cost is genuinely free here. A spare token is not a card — it is a renewable by-product, and the deck makes 6.63 bodies by turn 10 on average. Trade it for the class the deck is worst at finding: the drain, 60.8% unassisted. Bastion is the one to name for the reasons the verified boards give — 7 from each opponent, 28 across the pod (stack 002), an enchantment that dodges creature removal, and a free Human Soldier body on entry.

targets.scenario: Nest of Scarabs is already on the battlefield and you are hunting the kill. On board: Bloodghast, or Butcher Ghoul, or Carrier Thrall — a body that pays you back when it leaves.
targets.why: This is the pairing the deck was built for and almost nobody makes on purpose. Intent is the only wish that costs you the exact resource the Blowfly kill needs — bodies — so pay it with a body that returns. Bloodghast comes back on your next land drop. Butcher Ghoul comes back with undying. Carrier Thrall leaves an Eldrazi Scion behind. Your body count survives the tutor, which is what keeps stack 001's requirement intact: the drain plus two other creatures on the battlefield when the loop starts, then 38 iterations from 40 to 0.

targets.scenario: A sweeper just resolved. You have one creature left — Grave Titan, or any nonlegendary body — and Nest of Scarabs somehow survived because it is an enchantment.
targets.why: The rebuild that eats your own additional cost. Sacrifice the last body to Intent, then cast the two-mana sorcery that brings it straight back with a -1/-1 counter on it. Stack 006 verified the part that matters: a creature ENTERING with a -1/-1 counter does trigger Nest of Scarabs, via rule 122.6 — so Persist is reanimation and ignition in one card. Grave Titan returns as a 5/5 deathtoucher with two 2/2 Zombies and an Insect riding along. Know the trap the same stack found: Persist on Fume Spitter gives you the Insect and NOT the body, because a 1/1 entering as a 0/0 dies to state-based actions before the trigger resolves. Aim it at something with toughness to spare.

targets.scenario: Mikaeus, the Unhallowed is on the battlefield. Your non-Human creatures all have undying and +1/+1. You want a second engine and the table is watching Yawgmoth, not you.
targets.why: The wish nobody sees coming, because under Mikaeus the additional cost stops being a cost at all — sacrifice any non-Human and undying hands it straight back. Carnifex Demon is a Phyrexian Demon, so it joins that family, and its {B}, remove a -1/-1 counter ability puts a counter on EACH other creature: a table-wide shrink that is also a pile of Insects with Nest out. Straight talk about the ceiling: the Mikaeus two-card infinites this family implies set the deck's bracket floor and NOT ONE of them has been verified on this list, while three of the source's claims about this exact deck have already been overturned by the checker. Fetch the Demon for the board it builds. Treat the loop as a candidate, not a plan.

tutors.notes: The cost is upside when you have a token, a returning body, or a drain on the battlefield turning the sacrifice into damage. It is a tax in exactly three spots: when your only creature is the engine that makes the others, when you control no creature at all and the spell is simply uncastable, and on turn three — the sim has you at a mean of 1.70 bodies there, so Intent is often a dead card in an opening hand. And if Nest of Scarabs is the missing piece, it outranks everything on this list; make that wish with Vampiric or Demonic and keep your bodies.

targets.scenario: Turn 5 or 6 with four mana up and a token to spare — a Faerie, an Insect, a Treasure from Deadly Dispute or Black Market Connections. Yawgmoth is on the battlefield. The hub is missing.
targets.why: The default, and it is the best four mana in the deck. Bargain the token, search up Nest at mana value 3, and cast it FREE from exile — hub online the same turn, one card spent, and the token you paid was going to die to Yawgmoth anyway. The free-cast clause is capped at mana value 4 or less, which happens to cover every piece that matters: Nest, Blowfly Infestation, Bastion of Remembrance, Bitterblossom, both Altars, Toxic Deluge.

targets.scenario: You are behind. Player 1 has a wide board of tokens, Player 3 has two fat creatures, and the damage is coming at you. You have four mana, a spare token, and a drain already on the battlefield.
targets.why: The behind fetch. Bargain, find Deluge, cast it without paying its mana cost — you still pay the X life, because an additional cost is not the mana cost and the alternative cost does not touch it. Set X to whatever the table needs. Your board dies too, and that is the point: with an each-opponent drain out, your own sweeper meters every one of your deaths into damage, and your recursion rebuilds. One accuracy note so you sequence it right: Deluge gives -X/-X until end of turn, NOT -1/-1 counters, so it triggers nothing on Nest of Scarabs and returns nothing with Necroskitter.

citations.quote: An additional cost is a cost listed in a spell’s rules text, or applied to a spell or ability from another effect, that its controller must pay at the same time they pay the spell’s mana cost or the ability’s activation cost.
An alternative cost doesn’t change a spell’s mana cost, only what its controller has to pay to cast it.

targets.scenario: Yawgmoth is online and drawing you cards — the verified boards run him to eight activations and eight cards in one turn — and your hand is now full of spells you cannot cast. Four mana, one spare token.
targets.why: The odd wish, and it is the one that unlocks the turn you are actually having. Engine mana is a real hole on the sheet, 53.0% unassisted against 82.0% assisted, and it is the class that converts Yawgmoth's draws into castable spells. Bargain, find the Altar at mana value 3, cast it free: now every body you sacrifice is a black mana, and the cards Yawgmoth hands you stop being decoration. Ashnod's Altar is the fallback and pays colourless, which this mono-black list minds more than most.

targets.scenario: Late, grindy, and you are down to your last token. No fodder engine on the battlefield, no bodies in hand, four mana available.
targets.why: Spend your last body to buy a body every upkeep. Bargaining away the final token feels wrong and is right: Bitterblossom at mana value 2 comes in free and makes a 1/1 flier on every one of your upkeeps forever, for 1 life a turn. It is also an enchantment, so it survives the sweeper that is coming. Normally you never spend a wish on fodder — the class is 78.6% unassisted and the deck finds it alone — but a board with zero renewable bodies is outside that distribution, and the fodder is the enabler that gates everything else.

tutors.notes: Two disciplines. First, bargain fodder is a token or a Treasure, never Nest of Scarabs, never Bitterblossom, never the drain you just landed — sacrificing the engine to find the engine is the trap the card sets. Second, Mikaeus is mana value 6, so Beseech can never free-cast him; if Mikaeus is the wish, make it with Demonic, Vampiric or Insatiable Avarice and keep Beseech for a piece at 4 or less. And your commander lives in the command zone, not the library — no search in this deck finds Yawgmoth.

targets.scenario: Turn 6 or 7, five or six mana, board stable, engine grinding. Nothing in your hand costs more than three and you want a second axis.
targets.why: The default, once you understand what this tutor is actually for. Avarice is the slow wish — {B} plus {2} for the search mode, sorcery speed, to the TOP — so the transit turn is a real cost when the card is cheap and NO cost at all when the card is expensive. Mikaeus costs six; you were going to spend that turn making mana anyway. He hands every non-Human you control +1/+1 and undying, which is renewable fodder, free Diabolic Intent costs, and the second kill the sim tracks at 1.8% unassisted and 24.8% assisted. Take the honest caveat with him: that kill's two-card infinites are unverified on this list.

citations.quote: Spree means “Choose one or more modes. As an additional cost to cast this spell, pay the costs associated with those modes.”

targets.scenario: Turn 7 or later with five mana up. Yawgmoth and Nest are online, bodies are stacked, and the pod is still at 40 because nothing converts deaths into damage.
targets.why: Pay for both Spree modes — {B} plus {2} to search, plus {B}{B} for the draw — and the wish stops being an appointment. The modes execute in the order printed, so the search puts Zulaport on top and the draw-three picks it straight back up, with two extra cards and 3 life as the toll. That mode ordering is a coaching read on the printed sequence rather than a checker-verified ruling, so treat the sequencing as judgement. Zulaport itself is verified: 7 drains, 28 across the pod, and it caps at 7 precisely because it is a body that must eventually be sacrificed and banks its own death trigger last (stack 003). Two mana to deploy makes it the drain you can actually cast on the same turn you find it.

targets.scenario: A sweeper resolved two turns ago. Your graveyard is stocked, you are at seven-plus lands, and the table has moved on to fighting each other.
targets.why: The behind fetch that fits Avarice's shape. Six mana, three bodies on entry — a 6/6 deathtoucher and two 2/2 Zombies — and the transit turn overlaps the turn you spend getting to six anyway. It refills the fodder engine in one card, it blocks anything, and it is nonlegendary, so Persist and Victimize can bring it back after the NEXT sweeper. Board quantity is not usually how this deck wins, but after a wrath the fastest route back to a working engine is one card that is three bodies.

targets.scenario: Turn 5, three lands, you missed a drop and have a fistful of three-drops. Your graveyard already holds two or three creatures.
targets.why: The wish nobody sees coming, because it is two cards. Put it on top and next turn it is simply the land you needed — pay 3 life and it even enters untapped. Later in the game the same card is the front face: return any number of creatures from your graveyard that each have a different mana value X or less, which on a curve of 1s, 2s and 3s is a whole board off one spell. A tutor that fixes your mana now and rebuilds your board later is the best rate on the sheet when the sim has you hitting the turn-5 land drop only 68.9% of the time.

tutors.notes: Do not read this as a one-mana tutor. The search mode is {B} plus {2}, so it is three mana at sorcery speed and it cannot be fired at an end step the way Vampiric can. The {B}{B} mode also targets any player: pointed at an opponent it is three cards and 3 life for them, which is the cheapest political favour in the deck — and worth remembering when you need one seat to leave you alone for a turn.

gaps: No wish in this deck finds an artifact or enchantment answer, because none exists to find. The library has no counterspell, no artifact removal and no enchantment removal, and one graveyard answer in Bojuka Bog. Against a resolved Cursed Totem, Pithing Needle or Rest in Peace your outs are speed, politics and somebody else's removal. The tutors make you faster. They cannot make you broader.

No search finds your commander. Yawgmoth lives in the command zone, and every one of these five cards searches your LIBRARY. If he is answered, the wish is Phyrexian Reclamation while he is in the graveyard, or Lightning Greaves before he is targeted at all. Plan the insurance before the removal, not after.

Two of the five deliver to the top of the library. Vampiric Tutor is an instant, so its transit turn costs nothing when you fire it at the end step before your turn; Insatiable Avarice is a sorcery and cannot do that, so its wish is genuinely a turn away unless you pay for the draw mode too. A wish in transit can be answered — discard, a Bojuka Bog on your yard, a sweeper that changes what you needed. Fetch what is right for the board you will have, not the board you have.

Ophiomancer only makes a Snake 'if you control no Snakes', and South Wind Avatar is a Snake Spirit Avatar. Fetching one while the other is on the battlefield switches your largest renewable fodder source off. If the Avatar is already down, wish for a different drain; if Ophiomancer is ticking, the Avatar's 4 toughness — worth exactly +4 activations on the verified board, and its 'near-infinite' billing refuted (stack 005) — is not worth the Snake it costs you.

The Mikaeus family is a candidate, not a plan. Eight two-card infinites involving Mikaeus set this deck's bracket floor and not one has been verified on this list, while the checker has already overturned three of the source's claims about these exact cards — the Blowfly kill as printed (stack 001, unbounded but drainless on that board), Blood Artist as 'near-infinite' (stack 004, eight life), and South Wind Avatar's 'near-infinite' tag (stack 005, +4 activations). Fetch Mikaeus for undying and bodies, which are real. Do not announce a loop nobody has signed.

The Blowfly kill has a body tax and the tutor does not pay it. Stack 001 is precise: the loop needs the drain plus TWO other creatures on the battlefield when it starts, and then 38 iterations take four opponents from 40 to 0. Short a body, Blowfly Infestation is a three-mana enchantment that drains for three and stops. Count before you wish.

Nothing here fetches Mirkwood Bats as a payoff. Its trigger reads on token CREATION rather than death, which is the half of the Nest of Scarabs engine that currently goes unpaid, and that is exactly why the rate it would pay is loop-specific and still unverified. It is a fine card to draw. It is not yet a card to spend a wish on.

Necropotence and a top-of-library tutor argue with each other. Necropotence skips your draw step, so a card booked to the top by Vampiric Tutor or Insatiable Avarice does not simply arrive next turn — you pay life to exile it and it reaches your hand at your next end step. Sequence the wish before the enchantment, or use a tutor that delivers to hand.

Whether Spree's modes execute in printed order — search first, then draw three, so the Avarice both-modes line delivers to hand the same turn — is a plain reading of the card that no stack has settled here. The line is worth the mana either way; the timing claim deserves a scenario before it is printed as fact.
